newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Newtelco seeks 10-15 pct of Swiss telecoms market.
newsitem.headline: Newtelco seeks 10-15 pct of Swiss telecoms market.

text.p: Swiss telecommunications consortium Newtelco said it thought it could eventually wrest a 10 to 15 percent share of the domestic market from Swiss Telecom after the country liberalises the sector in 1998.

Tele Danmark (TDK) has a 29 percent stake and British Telecommunications Plc 20 percent of the group, launched last year by Swiss Federal Railways (SBB), Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) and Swiss retailer Migros.
Newtelco also plans to seek a bourse listing eventually, company officials said at a news conference.

They said Newtelco will seek operating licenses for both its land-line network and for mobile phones as it competes for business and residential customers against Swiss Telecom, which is to be partially privatised in 1998, and other newcomers.

"You expect the incumbent to lose 25 points of market share over 10 years," said Alfred Mockett, BT's managing director for global communications, drawing on the experience of other state providers in Europe who have lost their monopoly status.
"Ten to 15 percent (Newtelco market share) over a 10-year period would not be an unreasonable expectation," he said.
"We don't for the time being see going too far abroad, so our target market is definitely Switzerland and our target customers are both businesses and private," added Newtelco Chairman Josef Egger.
He said he expected competition to halve telecoms prices in Switzerland.
Company officials said they envisioned investing around 500 million Swiss francs ($338 million) and saw turnover of one billion.
Mockett said the future of the market depended on how Berne liberalised the sector but added it should be along the same lines as the European Union is moving.
"In a mature market there should be enough room for two or three viable alternatives to the incumbent. Beyond that I think it gets a bit speculative," he said.
Tele Danmark's chief operating officer Lars Gronberg pointed out that Sweden has 11 licenses for fixed networks and seven for mobile phones.
"You have all the global players there and it seems all the players are surviving. I think we expect the same thing will happen here in Switzerland and we look forward to that competition," he said.

Newtelco Chief Executive Hans Ivanovitch said the company would capitalise on BT's existing Swiss operations and enhance service to multinational customers as of January 1, then focus on building business with small and mid-sized companies.
"In a later phase we are going to extend our reach to the residential (sector)," he said. "We will look to be in position to provide a number of services as quickly as possible."
He said his greatest wish was to conclude an interconnectivity deal with the Swiss PTT as soon as possible.
SBB President Benedikt Weibel broke down the partners' contributions to Newtelco in this way:
- SBB will grant Newtelco non-exclusive rights for 30 years to lay telephone cable along its tracks. SBB will invest part of the proceeds from this in the company
- UBS will invest cash and telecommunications traffic it now carries for third parties on its internal Ubinet system
- Migros will contribute cash and marketing know-how
- Tele Danmark invests cash and guarantees future investment
- BT contributes BT Switzerland and grants Newtelco the exclusive rights to distribute Concert products in Switzerland
- SBB and UBS contribute their license for an automated teller machine network called Wanda
-- Michael Shields, Zurich newsroom +41 1 631 7340 ($ = 1.479 Swiss Francs)
